title: Nkyerɛnsɛm kwan so asɛm / Describing changes over time
bridge: In Twi, describing changes over time often involves specific temporal markers and verb constructions that differ from English. Unlike English, which relies heavily on auxiliary verbs like 'have' for perfect tenses, Twi uses the verb 'rei' (to go) to indicate completed actions. Additionally, Twi emphasizes the duration or progression of change more explicitly, often using adverbs like 'bere' (already) or 'nna' (now). Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'used to' or 'has been,' as Twi structures these ideas differently.
rule: To describe changes over time in Twi, use the verb 'rei' (to go) followed by the main verb in its base form to indicate a completed change (e.g., 'Ɔde rei' means 'It has changed'). For ongoing changes, use the present progressive form with 're' (e.g., 'Ɔrehyɛ' means 'It is changing'). Temporal adverbs like 'bere' (already), 'nna' (now), or 'da' (then) are essential to specify when the change occurred. For past changes, use 'ɔkyena' (formerly) or 'bere' to contrast with the present. Exceptions include irregular verbs like 'ba' (to come), which does not follow the 'rei' pattern.

concept_examples.translation: It has changed.

concept_examples.text: Bere a, ɔne me kwan.
concept_examples.translation: Formerly, he followed me.

concept_examples.text: Nna ɔrehyɛ paa.
concept_examples.translation: Now it is changing a lot.

concept_examples.text: Da ɔde rei ba.
concept_examples.translation: Then it had come.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'has changed' without using the Twi construction with 'rei.' The correct form requires 'rei' followed by the verb, and adverbs like 'paa' (a lot) come after the verb phrase.

title: Especulación y deducciones / Speculating and Making Deductions
bridge: In Twi, speculating and making deductions often rely on contextual cues and specific verb constructions, unlike English where modal verbs like 'might' or 'could' are commonly used. Twi uses the verb 'sɛ' (to be like) or 'bɛ' (will be) to express probability or uncertainty. Be cautious not to directly translate English modals, as Twi structures are more context-dependent and less explicit.
rule: To speculate or make deductions in Twi, use the following structures: 1) 'Sɛ + subject + verb' to express probability (e.g., 'Sɛ ɔbɛba' means 'He might come'). 2) 'Bɛ + subject + verb' for future uncertainty (e.g., 'Bɛyɛ dɛ' means 'It could happen'). 3) 'Ebi wɔ' or 'Ebia wɔ' for 'maybe' or 'perhaps'. Note that Twi often omits subjects when they are clear from context, unlike English.

concept_examples.text: Sɛ ɔbɛba a, yɛbɛka kwan.
concept_examples.translation: If he might come, we will wait.

concept_examples.text: Bɛyɛ dɛ ɔbɛhwehwɛ no.
concept_examples.translation: It could be that he will look for it.

concept_examples.translation: Maybe he will be there.

concept_examples.text: Sɛ ɔbɛte saa a, yɛbɛkɔ.
concept_examples.translation: If it might rain like that, we will go.

title: Kɔ so akyi a, sɛnnɛ / Expressing Regret and Hypothetical Situations
bridge: In Twi, expressing regret and hypothetical situations involves specific grammatical structures that differ from English. Unlike English, which often uses 'if' clauses or modal verbs like 'would,' Twi uses the particle 'sɛ' for hypothetical situations and the phrase 'kɔ so akyi a' to express regret. Be cautious not to directly translate English structures, as Twi relies on context and specific particles to convey these nuances.
rule: To express regret, use the phrase 'kɔ so akyi a' followed by the main clause. For hypothetical situations, use 'sɛ' followed by the conditional clause, then the main clause. The verb in the conditional clause remains in its base form. For past regrets, use the past tense in the main clause. Example: 'Sɛ me kɔe a, mɛhua' (If I had gone, I would have won).

title: Ntɛm nyɛnsɛn ne nnwim / Discussing Pros and Cons
bridge: In Twi, discussing advantages and disadvantages often involves specific structures like 'ntɛm' (advantage) and 'nnwim' (disadvantage), which are more explicit than English's 'pros and cons'. Twi speakers frequently use comparative particles like 'sɛ' to introduce contrasting ideas, unlike English where 'but' or 'however' are common. Be cautious of word order, as Twi often places the verb before the object, which can feel unnatural for English speakers.
rule: To discuss advantages and disadvantages in Twi, use 'Ntɛm no...' for advantages and 'Nnwim no...' for disadvantages. Comparative sentences often start with 'Sɛ...' to introduce a contrasting point. Ensure the verb follows the subject-object order, and use the appropriate tense markers. For example, 'Sɛ yɛbɛka ntɛm no, ...' (If we talk about the advantage, ...) and 'Nnwim no ara na ɛyɛ...' (The disadvantage is that...).

title: Kyerɛkyerɛm kɛse / Narrating a Story
bridge: In Twi, narrating a story involves a more communal and interactive style compared to English. Twi storytelling often includes direct audience engagement, using phrases like 'W'anim yɛ?' (Is it true?) to involve listeners. Unlike English, Twi narratives frequently use proverbs and idioms, which can be challenging for learners. Additionally, Twi lacks a strict subject-verb-object order, allowing for more flexibility in sentence structure, which might feel less linear than English storytelling.
rule: To narrate a story in Twi, use the past tense marker 'ɛ́' for verbs, e.g., 'Onyansa ɛ́kaa' (The fox said). Incorporate time markers like 'da' (day) or 'bere' (time) to set the scene. Use the conjunction 'na' (and) to connect events. Remember, Twi storytelling often includes moral lessons, so phrases like 'N'asɛm yi ne sɛ...' (The moral of this story is...) are common. Avoid direct translation of English idioms; instead, learn Twi equivalents.

concept_examples.text: Ɛda a ɛ́fɔ̃, mmofra no wɔ́kɔɔ baabi a ɛwɔ ́ kuro no mu.

title: Kɔkɔɔ kɛseɛ / Arguing a Point of View
bridge: In Twi, arguing a point of view involves a more communal and respectful approach compared to English. While English often uses direct confrontation, Twi relies on proverbs, indirect expressions, and appeals to shared values. Avoid being overly assertive, as it may be perceived as disrespectful. Additionally, Twi uses specific verb forms and sentence structures to express disagreement politely, which differ from English’s more straightforward 'I disagree.'
rule: To argue a point of view in Twi, use expressions like 'Mɛma me ka' (Let me say) or 'Mɛyɛ biribi bi' (I’ll say something) to introduce your opinion. Follow with 'Na me nte' (Because I think) or 'Ɛda adi mfe' (It’s better if) to support your argument. Use proverbs (mmetan) to strengthen your point. Avoid direct contradictions; instead, use phrases like 'Ɛnyɛ nokware' (It’s not true) followed by 'Nokwarem no yɛ...' (The truth is...). Polite disagreement is key, and tone matters more than in English.

title: Kɔkɔɔbɔ sɛnkyerɛnneɛ / Talking about work and career
bridge: In Twi, discussing work and career involves specific vocabulary and sentence structures that differ from English. For instance, Twi often uses verb prefixes to indicate the subject, unlike English where subject pronouns are more common. Additionally, Twi emphasizes respect and hierarchy in professional contexts, which may require specific expressions. Be cautious of direct translations, as they can sound unnatural in Twi.
rule: When talking about work and career in Twi, use the verb 'kɔ' (to go) to indicate going to work, followed by the location or profession. For example, 'Mekɔ sɔhwɛ' means 'I go to work as a teacher.' To describe your role, use the structure 'Me ka sɛ...' (I am called...). For past experiences, use the past tense marker 'na' or 'nnɛ'. Remember, Twi often omits subject pronouns when the context is clear, unlike English.

concept_examples.text: Mekɔ sɔhwɛ wɔ Adum.
concept_examples.translation: I work as a teacher in Adum.

concept_examples.text: Me ka sɛ ɔbɛkra.
concept_examples.translation: I am called a doctor.

title: Wɔfa a wɔyɛ / Describing Processes
bridge: In Twi, describing processes often involves using the verb 'yɛ' (to do) in a continuous or habitual sense, which differs from English where we might use the present simple or present continuous. Twi also uses specific particles like 'wɔ' to indicate the subject of the action, which is not directly translatable to English. Be cautious not to overuse 'yɛ' as it can sound repetitive; instead, vary your sentences with adverbs or conjunctions.
rule: To describe processes in Twi, use the structure 'Wɔfa a wɔyɛ...' (The way they do it...). The verb 'yɛ' is often followed by a noun or another verb in its infinitive form. For sequential actions, use conjunctions like 'na' (and) or 'a' (and then). Adverbs like 'daidaa' (quickly) or 'pɛpɛɛpɛ' (slowly) can modify the action. Remember, Twi sentences often omit the subject if it’s clear from context, unlike English where the subject is usually explicit.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often translate 'do' directly to 'yɛ' and add unnecessary subjects. In Twi, the subject is often implied, and 'na' (and) or 'a' (and then) is used to connect actions without repeating the subject.

examples.original: Kɔso kɔso, wɔde nsuo ma ahɔɔ.
examples.phonetic: kɔso kɔso, vɔde nsuo ma ahɔɔ
examples.translation: Step by step, they use water to clean it.
examples.note: Use 'kɔso kɔso' to emphasize sequential actions.

examples.original: Ɛda a ɛbɛyɛ no, ɛsɛe mmienu.
examples.phonetic: ɛda a ɛbɛjɛ no, ɛsɛe mmienu
examples.translation: The way you do it, add two.
examples.note: Focus on the action and its immediate consequence.

examples.translation: They fill it out and submit.
examples.note: Use 'na' to connect two related actions.

examples.translation: Add and stir.
examples.note: Keep sentences concise and action-focused.

examples.translation: They do it quickly.
examples.note: Add adverbs like 'daidaa' to modify the action.

examples.translation: Do it slowly and it will turn out well.
examples.note: Combine adverbs with outcomes for richer descriptions.

title: Sɛe mmɔdenkyem / Expressing Uncertainty
bridge: In Twi, expressing uncertainty often involves modal verbs and specific particles like 'sɛ' and 'nea'. Unlike English, where 'maybe' or 'perhaps' are common, Twi uses structures that directly indicate doubt or probability. Be cautious not to overuse 'sɛ' as it can sound overly tentative, and remember that word order is more flexible in Twi, allowing emphasis on uncertainty.
rule: To express uncertainty in Twi, use the particle 'sɛ' before the verb to indicate possibility or doubt. For example, 'Sɛ me rekɔ' means 'I might go'. For higher uncertainty, use 'nea' with the verb, e.g., 'Nea ɛbɛyɛ' means 'It might happen'. Additionally, the word 'anka' can be used to express 'maybe' or 'perhaps'. Note that Twi relies heavily on context, so the tone and situation often clarify the degree of uncertainty.

concept_examples.text: Sɛ ɛbɛba paa.
concept_examples.translation: He might come indeed.

concept_examples.text: Anka mɛfa akɔnta no.
concept_examples.translation: Maybe I’ll take the account.

concept_examples.text: Nea ɛbɛyɛ a, ɛyɛ den.
concept_examples.translation: If it happens, it’s good.

concept_examples.text: Sɛ obi bɛma me.
concept_examples.translation: Someone might help me.

common_error.wrong: I maybe go to the market.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'maybe' or 'perhaps' without using the correct Twi structures. In Twi, 'sɛ' or 'anka' must be used to express uncertainty, and the word order should follow Twi grammar rules.

examples.translation: It might rain.
examples.note: Use 'sɛ' before the verb to express possibility.

examples.translation: He might come.
examples.note: Simple structure for everyday use.

examples.translation: Maybe I’ll eat.
examples.note: Use 'anka' for informal uncertainty.

examples.translation: Maybe it will happen.
examples.note: Common in casual conversations.

examples.translation: If it happens, it’s good.
examples.note: Use 'nea' for conditional uncertainty.

examples.original: Nea obi bɛma me a, mɛkɔ.
examples.phonetic: nea obi bɛma me a, mɛkɔ
examples.translation: If someone helps me, I’ll go.
examples.note: Complex structure for higher CEFR B1 level.

title: Kɔkɔɔbɔ sɛnkyerɛnee / Formal Requests
bridge: In Twi, making formal requests involves specific polite expressions and verb constructions that differ from English. Unlike English, where 'please' is often added at the end, Twi uses dedicated verbs and particles to convey politeness. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'Can you help me?' as they may sound informal or inappropriate in Twi. Additionally, Twi formal requests often include honorific titles, which are less common in English.
rule: To make a formal request in Twi, use the verb 'hwɛ' (to ask) or 'sɛ' (to request) followed by the object and the polite particle 'na'. For example, 'Hwɛ ma me' means 'Please help me.' Another common structure is 'De ma me...' (Please give me...). Always include honorific titles like 'Nana' (chief) or 'Opanin/Opanyin' (elder) when addressing someone formally. Avoid using the informal 'wo' (you) and instead use 'wɔ' or the person's title.

concept_examples.text: Hwɛ ma me kɔkɔɔbɔ no na.
concept_examples.translation: Please give me the form.

concept_examples.text: De ma me nsɛm pii na.
concept_examples.translation: Please tell me more.

concept_examples.text: Opanin, sɛ ma me akɔnta no na.
concept_examples.translation: Elder, please give me the account.
concept_examples.phonetic: /opanin, sɛ ma me akɔnta no na/

concept_examples.text: Nana, hwɛ ma me nkyɛn na.
concept_examples.translation: Chief, please help me.

common_error.correct: Hwɛ ma me kɔkɔɔbɔ no na.
common_error.explanation: Directly translating 'Can you help me?' into Twi sounds informal and may be perceived as rude. Instead, use the polite structures 'Hwɛ ma me...' or 'De ma me...' to convey respect and formality.

examples.original: De ma me kyerɛw no na.

examples.translation: Please give me the book.

examples.original: Hwɛ ma me pen no na.
examples.translation: Please give me the pen.
examples.note: Always include 'no' (the) for specificity.

examples.original: Opanin, sɛ ma me ntɔ no na.
examples.phonetic: /opanin, sɛ ma me ntɔ no na/
examples.translation: Elder, please fix it for me.
examples.note: Use honorific titles and 'sɛ' for services.
